chapters.title: Chapter 5: Scaling Playbook: Growing AUM Without Killing the Edge

lessons.title: Scaling Across Instruments: Cash, Futures, and Multiple Market-Cap Segments

children.text: The last lesson scaled by running different strategies side by side. This lesson scales the same underlying idea by changing where and how it is expressed, across market-cap segments and across cash versus futures, a lever that needs far less new research but comes with its own honest limits.

The same methodology, the same style of screen or ranking, can often be applied separately to large-cap, mid-cap, and small-cap universes. Because the actual securities in each tier are entirely different companies, position overlap between the three sleeves is genuinely low, close to the ideal condition from the last lesson, even though it is really one idea running three times rather than three independently researched strategies.

body.caption: A common, general pattern across market-cap tiers

cells: High, deep liquidity across the board
Lower per-stock alpha, a more efficiently priced market
Potentially higher per-stock alpha, less efficiently priced

body.text: Position overlap between the three sleeves is low, but crowding risk is not automatically low along with it. If the underlying methodology itself becomes popular, other desks can end up applying the same style of screen to the same three segments at the same time, reintroducing the correlated risk from Chapter 3 even though no single stock is shared between your own three books.

children.text: Lever Two: Cash vs Futures, the Same Exposure Through a Different Door

For stocks eligible for futures trading on the NSE, a category the exchange and SEBI define using market-wide position limits and liquidity criteria, so it covers only a subset of listed companies, generally the larger and more liquid ones, the same directional view can be expressed either in the cash market or through the stock's futures contract. These are two distinct order books, so splitting an order across both can draw on more standalone liquidity than working either book alone.

columns.label: Cash Market
points: Available for every listed NSE stock
One order book, no expiry or rollover to manage
Liquidity is whatever the cash market itself offers

columns.label: Stock Futures
points: Only margin required, more capital-efficient exposure
Available only for F&O-eligible stocks, a subset chosen by liquidity criteria
A separate order book, but with expiry and rollover to manage
Adds a second, distinct pool of liquidity for the same underlying exposure

body.text: Cash and futures prices for the same stock are kept in line by arbitrageurs constantly trading the spread between them, the basis. That link means the two books are not fully independent liquidity pools the way two genuinely different strategies can be. Splitting execution across both reduces the impact felt in either single book and can meaningfully help at the margin, but it is not the same kind of clean capacity addition described in the previous lesson, and it adds its own complexity around basis risk and rollover near expiry.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: A trader argues that splitting a large stock purchase evenly between the cash market and the stock's futures contract effectively doubles the strategy's true capacity, since two separate order books are now involved. Is this reasoning sound?
options: Yes, because cash and futures are completely separate, unrelated liquidity pools

No, because cash and futures for the same stock are linked by arbitrage, so splitting execution can meaningfully reduce impact on either book but does not create a fully independent second pool of capacity
No, because SEBI prohibits trading the same stock in both cash and futures at the same time
Yes, but only for small-cap stocks
body.explanation: Arbitrage keeps cash and futures prices tied together through the basis, so the two books are related, not independent. Splitting execution across both is a genuine, useful technique for reducing single-book impact, but it does not create the kind of clean, additive capacity that two genuinely uncorrelated strategies can, as covered in the previous lesson.

children.text: A scaled Indian quant desk might run parallel sleeves of one methodology across large-cap, mid-cap, and small-cap tiers, and within the large-cap sleeve, additionally split execution between cash and futures for the most liquid, F&O-eligible names. Combined, these two levers can meaningfully expand capacity beyond a single-instrument, single-segment book, without requiring a single new signal to be researched, provided both the crowding caveat from segment stratification and the arbitrage caveat from cash-futures splitting are taken seriously rather than assumed away.

body.text: You do not always need a new idea to scale. The same idea, applied across market-cap tiers or split across cash and futures, can absorb more capital than a single instrument in a single segment ever could, as long as you are honest about how much of that extra room is genuinely independent and how much is only partially so.

points: Running the same methodology separately across large-cap, mid-cap, and small-cap tiers achieves low position overlap cheaply, since the underlying securities are entirely different, though shared methodology can still reintroduce crowding risk across tiers.
Futures are available only for a subset of NSE stocks meeting exchange and SEBI liquidity criteria, and offer a distinct order book alongside the cash market for the same underlying exposure.

Cash and futures liquidity for the same stock are linked by arbitrage, so splitting execution across both reduces single-book impact meaningfully but does not create a fully independent second pool of capacity.

Both levers, segment stratification and cash-futures splitting, are genuinely useful for scaling without new research, provided their respective caveats, crowding and basis linkage, are actively monitored rather than assumed away.
